title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
text: A perfect morning can unravel in seconds. You stride into class brimming with energy—whiteboard ready, slides synced, a killer opener on your tongue. Five minutes later a desk screeches, a paper missile arcs overhead, or a snarky whisper ignites giggles. Instinct shouts How dare you! Yet the real breakthrough begins when you bite back the reprimand and instead ask, Why is this happening? That single question shifts the focus from punishment to possibility.

Five minutes later a desk screeches, a paper missile arcs overhead, or a snarky whisper ignites giggles. Instinct shouts How dare you! Yet the real breakthrough begins when you bite back the reprimand and instead ask, Why is this happening? That single question shifts the focus from punishment to possibility.

title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
text:
Unmasking the Message Behind Misbehaviour
What we brand as troublemaking often hides an unmet need. A student who interrupts loudly may crave recognition because invisibility feels worse than a scolding. Relentless fidgeting can mask anxiety or sensory overload; sarcastic retorts are armor against shame; chronic lateness might stem from exhaustion, caregiving duties, or lingering sadness. Sometimes the root is academic—an idea missed weeks ago turns embarrassment into sabotage. Home stress, online bullying, identity-testing adolescence, or undiagnosed neurodiversity can all masquerade as defiance. When we read behaviour as communication, the entire classroom conversation changes.

title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
text:
Turning Disruption into Dialogue
Transformation starts with small, consistent moves. Begin each day with a two-minute greeting ritual that fills attention “tanks” before they run dry. Braid autonomy into lessons—let learners choose between a written reflection or an audio note so power struggles never start. Schedule quick “brain breaks” so pent-up energy escapes constructively, and agree on subtle hand signals that curb off-task chatter without public shaming. When a line is crossed, a brief restorative chat—What happened, who was affected, how do we fix it—replaces the sting of a lecture with a chance to repair.

title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
section: From Class Clown to Classroom Leader
text:
From Class Clown to Classroom Leader
Back in my own classroom, there was a child—an eighth-grader who had an uncanny ability to derail a lesson in seconds. I tried gentle dialogues, firm reminders, even strategic seating; nothing held. With grades due and projects piling up, I eventually let the behaviour slide and walked away feeling I’d failed him. Only once I stepped outside that whirlwind did I see it differently: That child’s punchlines were really a bid for connection, not defiance. That hindsight fuels this series—practical reflections I wish someone had handed me while I was still in the thick of it, and that I now offer to anyone navigating similar moments with children.

title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
text:
The Teacher’s Self-Reflection Lens
Before managing anyone else, regulate yourself. A calm tone and relaxed posture model the control you hope students will find. Offer dignified exits rather than ultimatums—“Need a minute in the hallway or prefer to talk after class?”—so students keep their dignity intact. Learn one non-academic fact about each child; relationship is the currency of influence. Finally, ask whether any consequence you impose actually teaches or merely punishes. If it fails that test, revisit your strategy.

title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
text:
When Empathy Needs Reinforcements
Even the best intentions sometimes fall short. That’s when documentation and collaboration count: track patterns and share them with counselors and caregivers who can reveal hidden triggers. Invite a trusted colleague to observe your class; another pair of eyes often spots what yours miss. Most crucially, guard your own rest. Chronic fatigue is empathy’s worst enemy, and without empathy, curiosity collapses into control.

title: Troublemakers? Yes. But Why?!
text:
The Real Question, Revisited
So the next time a student derails your flow, remember the essential pivot: not “How dare you?” but “Why do you need to act this way to be heard?” Ask it sincerely and you’ll uncover stories that humble and inspire. As a personal challenge, pause after your next disruption, jot down the possible reasons behind it, and watch the narrative shift from discipline to understanding, from control to connection. The transformation starts with one deliberate breath—and one honest Why?

Originally published on LinkedIn, 3 August 2025.

title: The Power of Pause: Responding Instead of Reacting
text: In the fast pace of a classroom, teachers are often expected to think, decide, and act in split seconds. A student mutters under their breath, another refuses to participate, a group becomes restless — and instinct tells us to react immediately to restore order. Yet in those moments, the most powerful tool a teacher has is not a sharp reprimand or an instant correction. It is the pause.

title: The Power of Pause: Responding Instead of Reacting
text:
Why the Pause Matters
Children’s behaviours, whether disruptive or withdrawn, are rarely random. They often carry traces of anxiety, fatigue, insecurity, or unmet needs. When teachers react impulsively, we address only the surface behaviour, not the underlying cause. Worse, an instant reaction may escalate tension, embarrass the student publicly, or break the trust we are trying to build.
Pausing gives us time to:

Reframe the situation — shifting from “How dare they?” to “What could have led to this response?”
Control the emotional climate — as adults, our tone sets the room’s temperature.
Model self-regulation — students notice not just what we teach, but how we manage our own impulses.

In this sense, a pause is not hesitation or weakness. It is a deliberate act of professional strength.

title: The Power of Pause: Responding Instead of Reacting
text:
Silence as a Pedagogical Tool
A moment of silence in class is often misread as wasted time. In truth, silence can be deeply instructive. A pause before speaking gives:

Students time to reflect on what just happened, often leading to self-correction.
Teachers space to choose words carefully, preventing unnecessary harshness.
The whole class a reset, stopping potential escalation before it spreads.

When silence is used intentionally, it transforms into a signal of presence and control, rather than passivity.

title: The Power of Pause: Responding Instead of Reacting
text:
Practical Strategies for Teachers

Micro-pauses: Before addressing behaviour, take a slow breath in and out. This brief act often prevents tone from tipping into irritation.
Time-shifted conversations: Instead of reacting in the heat of the lesson, use non-verbal signals to acknowledge behaviour and speak privately after class. This preserves dignity and prevents disruption.
Written cues: Slip a short note — “I see you’re upset, we’ll talk later” — instead of verbal correction. This acknowledges the student without putting them on display.
Transparent modelling: Share with your class that teachers, too, take a breath before responding. This normalizes pausing as an everyday skill, not just a teacher’s technique.
Structured waiting: After asking a question or giving an instruction, count silently to five before repeating or rephrasing. This respects processing time for students who need longer to respond.

title: The Power of Pause: Responding Instead of Reacting
section: The Ripple Effect on Classroom Culture
text:
The Ripple Effect on Classroom Culture
When a teacher demonstrates that strong emotions or challenging behaviours do not demand instant retaliation, students learn an invaluable lesson: self-control. They begin to see that emotions can be acknowledged, contained, and then expressed thoughtfully. Over time, classrooms built on this rhythm of pausing become calmer, more respectful, and more resilient.
This practice extends beyond behaviour management. It shapes how children handle disagreements with peers, how they respond to stress, and how they build empathy. By watching us pause, they internalize that being human is not about avoiding emotion but about responding to it wisely.

title: The Power of Pause: Responding Instead of Reacting
text:
Closing Reflection
Empathy in education is not only expressed through what we say but also when and how we say it. The pause may seem like a small gap in a busy classroom day, yet it is in that gap that understanding grows. Choosing to respond rather than react is one of the quietest, but most profound, ways to teach.

title: Parent-Teacher Partnerships: Aligning Communication for a Child’s Growth
text: We often talk about a child’s growth as if it happens in separate silos—home, school, society. But a child doesn’t experience life in compartments. Their thoughts, emotions, and behaviors travel with them from classroom to living room, from the dinner table to the school desk. That’s why a strong, empathetic partnership between parents and teachers is not optional—it’s essential.

title: Parent-Teacher Partnerships: Aligning Communication for a Child’s Growth
section: The Problem: Misaligned Intentions, Misunderstood Actions
text:
The Problem: Misaligned Intentions, Misunderstood Actions
Many teachers feel that parents don’t understand the school’s expectations. Many parents feel that teachers don’t understand their child. Somewhere in this gap, the child gets caught.

A parent may shield their child from consequences, thinking they’re protecting self-esteem.
A teacher may enforce strict discipline, believing it builds responsibility.
Both may be right—from their own perspectives—but without shared communication, the child receives mixed signals.

title: Parent-Teacher Partnerships: Aligning Communication for a Child’s Growth
text:
Empathy as a Communication Lens
Empathy doesn’t mean agreeing. It means listening without judgment, seeking to understand before reacting.

Teachers, when reaching out, try asking: “What have you noticed at home?” before explaining what’s happening at school.
Parents, when concerned, try asking: “What’s your observation of my child in class?” rather than starting with complaints.

This shifts the tone from accusation to collaboration.

title: Parent-Teacher Partnerships: Aligning Communication for a Child’s Growth
section: Every Educator Counts: A Unified Support System
text:
Every Educator Counts: A Unified Support System
The class teacher, often serving as the consistent adult presence across the year, becomes the coordinator and emotional anchor. They help connect academic, behavioral, and social dots, mediating between the school’s values and the home’s expectations.
Subject teachers are often the most visible academic guides in a child’s school life. But their role goes far beyond delivering lessons — they observe emotional responses to challenges, patterns of motivation, group behavior, and emerging leadership or withdrawal. Their insights are foundational to a child’s development.
Language teachers, in particular, play a dual role. Not only do they build the foundational skills of communication—reading, writing, expression—but they also serve as gateways to cultural understanding and emotional literacy. Through stories, discussions, and reflective writing, they help children process emotions, empathize with different perspectives, and navigate identity—skills essential for emotional intelligence and respectful peer interactions.
At the same time, P.E., art, music, and club activity educators engage the child in expressive, creative, and physical domains. In these spaces, children may reveal aspects of themselves unseen in a traditional classroom — a hesitant speaker might sing freely, a distracted student might focus deeply while painting. These teachers complete the picture and their observations are invaluable in forming a holistic understanding of the child.
Together, all educators — academic, pastoral, co-curricular, and linguistic — form a collaborative circle around the child. Their combined perspectives, when shared empathetically with parents, ensure no potential goes unnoticed and no concern is dismissed.

title: Parent-Teacher Partnerships: Aligning Communication for a Child’s Growth
section: Building the Bridge: Practical Empathetic Strategies
text:
Building the Bridge: Practical Empathetic Strategies

Set Common Goals Early On At the beginning of the academic year, co-create shared goals—not just academic, but behavioral, emotional, and social. Make the child the center of this vision.
Replace Blame with Curiosity Instead of saying, “Why did the teacher scold you again?”, ask, “What do you think happened in class today?” Similarly, instead of, “Your child never listens,” say, “I noticed this pattern. Have you seen it too?”
Respect Both Contexts Teachers should recognize that home may carry unseen stressors. Parents should acknowledge the challenges of managing multiple children in a class. Mutual respect opens the door to trust.
Create Multiple Channels for Ongoing Dialogue Not every conversation needs to be a formal meeting. Voice notes, emails, shared behavior logs, or quick check-ins after school can maintain steady communication.
Include All Stakeholders Invite co-curricular, language, and subject teachers into the communication loop—especially when discussing a child’s emotional, behavioral, or creative patterns. Their input often reveals untapped strengths or hidden emotional signals.
Celebrate Together Don’t wait for problems to talk. Celebrate effort, kindness, improvement—not just grades. Shared joy builds a foundation for future conflict resolution.

title: Parent-Teacher Partnerships: Aligning Communication for a Child’s Growth
section: Conclusion: A Unified Circle Around the Child
text:
Conclusion: A Unified Circle Around the Child
When parents and teachers stand on opposite shores, the child is forced to swim alone. But when we build a bridge of empathetic communication, we create a circle of care—one that supports the child from all sides.
The subject teacher nurtures learning. The class teacher connects the dots. The language teacher gives voice and context. The co-curricular educators add expression and texture. And parents bring the child’s lived experience. Together, they form a complete and nurturing ecosystem.
Empathy isn’t soft. It’s strategic. It doesn’t eliminate discipline or expectations—it gives them meaning. And when parents and all educators speak in harmony, the child grows not just academically, but emotionally secure and socially aware

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
text:
Not every student raises their hand when they’re struggling. Sometimes, the loudest cries come in silence.
As educators, we are trained to listen. We listen to questions, concerns, answers, and outbursts. But in the everyday rhythm of teaching, what often goes unnoticed is the absence of communication — the unspoken hesitations, the quiet disengagement, the subtle tension behind a smile.
These silent struggles carry more weight than we might think. And it’s here that empathy becomes our most vital tool.

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
text:
Why Some Struggles Remain Silent
Children are not always equipped with the emotional vocabulary to express what’s troubling them. Others may fear being judged or misunderstood. Some have been conditioned to believe that their struggles are theirs to bear — quietly, invisibly.
Here are a few reasons why students may not speak up:

Fear of ridicule or embarrassment in front of peers.
Cultural or familial expectations discouraging open emotional expression.
Previous experiences where opening up did not lead to support.
Unawareness — not realizing what they feel can be discussed.

As teachers, the first step is to become attuned to these hidden cues.

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
section: Signs to Look For: Non-Verbal Red Flags
text:
Signs to Look For: Non-Verbal Red Flags
Empathetic teaching means noticing when something feels off. Here are some subtle signs that may signal a student is silently struggling:

Sudden drop in participation or academic performance.
Changes in posture — withdrawn body language, avoidance of eye contact.
Overcompensation — forced cheerfulness, excessive perfectionism.
Consistent fatigue or appearing distracted, even disengaged.
Repeatedly forgetting materials, homework, or tasks.
Clashes with peers or unexpected outbursts.

No single sign confirms a deeper issue — but a combination often points toward a need for intervention.

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
text:
Responding with Empathy, Not Interrogation
Once we sense a student might be going through something, how we respond can either open a door or shut it forever.

Create private moments: A quiet word after class often speaks louder than a public check-in.
Use gentle prompts: Instead of asking “What’s wrong?”, try “You seem a little distant today — want to talk?”
Validate before advising: Acknowledge their emotions before trying to “fix” anything.
Respect their pace: Don’t force disclosure. Sometimes, just being available is enough.

The goal isn’t always to extract answers. It’s to assure them: You’re not alone here.

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
section: Building a Classroom That Listens Without Pressure
text:
Building a Classroom That Listens Without Pressure
To support silent strugglers, we must build an environment where speaking up feels safe.

Normalize emotional check-ins: Simple practices like mood boards, anonymous boxes, or reflection journals can invite quiet students to share in their own way.
Model vulnerability: When teachers share their own challenges (within healthy boundaries), it builds mutual trust.
Celebrate listening: Reinforce that empathy among peers is just as valuable as academic achievement.
Train yourself: Professional development in emotional intelligence and trauma-informed practices can be invaluable.

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
text:
Empathy Doesn’t Always Need Words
At the heart of this approach is a shift — from seeing students as learners to seeing them as people. From reacting to behavior, to understanding its cause. From assuming, to observing. From instructing, to listening — even when no words are spoken.
The quietest child in your class may be screaming on the inside. Let your presence be the answer they didn’t know they were looking for.

title: Listening Beyond Words: Recognizing Silent Struggles in the Classroom
text:
Final Thought
Empathy isn’t a soft skill. It’s a survival tool in today’s classroom — for both teachers and students. By listening beyond words, we don’t just bridge communication gaps — we build bridges of trust, safety, and growth.

title: Equity in Expression: Giving Every Child a Voice
text:
No matter how boisterous a classroom is, how lively the atmosphere, or how engaged the discussion feels, there is almost always one child who chooses silence. They sit quietly, listening, observing, but rarely speaking—even when gently encouraged to do so.
Instead of accepting this silence as mere preference, empathy asks us to pause and wonder: Why? Is it fear of judgment? A history of being overlooked? A lack of confidence in language? Or simply a different way of processing the world?
When we ask these questions, we begin to see silence not as absence, but as presence in another form. And then the real challenge emerges: How can we invite such children into expression without burdening them, and without dampening the natural rhythm of the class?

When we ask these questions, we begin to see silence not as absence, but as presence in another form. And then the real challenge emerges: How can we invite such children into expression without burdening them, and without dampening the natural rhythm of the class?

title: Equity in Expression: Giving Every Child a Voice
text:
Why Equity in Expression Matters
Every child carries a voice, whether audible or quiet and that voice is tied to their sense of self-worth. If classrooms consistently privilege the loudest voices, we unintentionally send the message that only some thoughts are worth hearing. Over time, this erodes not just academic engagement but also confidence and belonging.
Equity in expression ensures that each learner knows: your words matter, your perspective counts, and your silence does not make you invisible.
Encouraging expression is also preparation for life beyond school. While silence may be a child’s preference, not every environment outside the classroom will honor that choice. The world they step into is often competitive, fast-paced, and less empathetic. As teachers, our responsibility is not only to respect quietness but also to equip children to express themselves confidently, irrespective of the mode of expression. This way, they are ready to navigate both supportive spaces and more challenging ones with dignity and courage.

title: Equity in Expression: Giving Every Child a Voice
section: Strategies for Welcoming the Silent Traveller
text:
Strategies for Welcoming the Silent Traveller
Multiple pathways for expression Not all contributions must be verbal. Journals, drawings, digital platforms, or anonymous question slips allow quieter students to express themselves without immediate spotlight.
Gentle structures Techniques like think-pair-share or round-robin sharing reduce pressure, giving quieter students time to prepare and space to contribute.
Mindful facilitation Keep track of who speaks often and who rarely does. Invite the quiet child with warmth, not command: “Would you like to share your thought?” rather than “Tell us now.”
Normalize imperfection Silence often comes from fear of being wrong. Emphasizing that mistakes are part of learning makes speaking up safer.
Value small steps A single sentence from a hesitant child is a big step. Celebrate it, without exaggeration or patronizing.
Model listening Teach peers to listen attentively and acknowledge contributions. Respect in the room amplifies even the quietest voice.

title: Equity in Expression: Giving Every Child a Voice
text:
The Empathetic Mindset
The goal is not to transform every silent traveller into a constant speaker. Some children will always lean toward quiet reflection, and that too is valid. The aim is to ensure their silence is a choice, not a consequence of fear, exclusion, or invisibility.
When teachers consciously make space for quieter voices, we build a classroom culture where every child belongs, not because they fit a mold, but because their unique way of engaging is valued. And when a silent traveller finally chooses to speak, the classroom learns that listening deeply can be as powerful as speaking often.
In the end, equity in expression is not just about classroom participation. It is about shaping confident, empathetic individuals who know their voice has value: whether spoken loudly, written quietly, or expressed creatively. That is the true gift of empathetic teaching.

title: What Do a Pan Masala Brand, a Betting App, and an Entrance Coaching Institution Have in Common?
text:
Wait… Before taking out your swords and guns, first read this and then decide.
At the core, all three — Pan Masala brands, betting apps, and coaching institutions — are businesses. Their foundation rests on a simple equation: profit and loss.
Still not convinced? Let’s talk numbers.
All three are billion-dollar industries with a shared obsession for visibility. A significant share of their spending goes into marketing and brand promotion.
But here’s the catch: these success stories are often statistical outliers. They’re not representative of the entire student base. The product being sold is not “education” — it’s aspiration, packaged and branded like toothpaste or cola.

title: What Do a Pan Masala Brand, a Betting App, and an Entrance Coaching Institution Have in Common?
text:
The Walking Ads
Step outside during school or coaching hours, and you’ll notice a branding masterstroke at play: students as moving billboards.

Schools are subtle, adding logos to shirts or chest pockets.
Coaching centers are brazen. Students wear uniforms with giant brand names across the back and front — bright, attention-grabbing colors walking in groups through cities.

And this visibility? It’s not free.
Even when uniforms are marketed as “included” or “free,” the cost is adjusted elsewhere — tucked into admission fees, service charges, or study material packages. Parents pay to make their child a dynamic banner. It’s smart marketing, yes — but deeply exploitative in spirit.

title: What Do a Pan Masala Brand, a Betting App, and an Entrance Coaching Institution Have in Common?
text:
Manufactured Merit
Ever seen the same student being promoted by multiple coaching institutes? It happens. A lot.
Institutes often:

Share credit for a student who attended their test series, crash course, or interview prep.
Retroactively claim toppers through paid associations or photo rights.

It’s not unlike a celebrity promoting multiple brands — only this time, the product is a child.

title: What Do a Pan Masala Brand, a Betting App, and an Entrance Coaching Institution Have in Common?
text:
The Emotional Cost
Unlike Pan Masala or betting apps, coaching institutions have a sheen of legitimacy — they’re “education providers.” But their impact can be equally damaging, just more insidious.
Children as young as 11 or 12 enter coaching pipelines. For the next few years, they live a life that is:

Conditioned, not nurtured.
Focused on performance, not self-discovery.
Tied to a narrow definition of success: crack the exam, or you’ve failed.

The years spent in this system coincide with some of the most formative stages of emotional development. But mental health? Resilience training? Emotional intelligence?
Nowhere in the curriculum.
Once the entrance exam is cleared, the institute’s job is done. No one tracks whether these children:

Thrive emotionally or academically in the long run.
Enter careers they’re passionate about.
Feel a sense of identity beyond a roll number and rank.

title: What Do a Pan Masala Brand, a Betting App, and an Entrance Coaching Institution Have in Common?
section: The Silence We Don’t Talk About
text:
The Silence We Don’t Talk About
We’ve all heard of suicide cases in places like Kota. But those are just the ones that make headlines.
What about:

The students who suffer quietly — slipping into anxiety, depression, or emotional shutdown?
The countless stories that go unreported, dismissed as just “stress” or “part of the process”?

And here’s what’s often overlooked:

The stress doesn’t disappear after success — it follows them.

Many students carry that pressure into college, unsure of who they are beyond a rank. After years of chasing a goal, they reach it — and find burnout, imposter syndrome, or a void where purpose should be.
Their stories aren’t individual failures. They are symptoms of a system that confuses performance with potential, and forgets to ask if the child is okay once the rank is achieved.

title: What Do a Pan Masala Brand, a Betting App, and an Entrance Coaching Institution Have in Common?
text:
My Take
Sure, not all coaching institutes are alike. Some are genuinely committed to education and equity. But those are exceptions — not the norm.
When profit becomes the driving force — even in education — then it’s no longer about learning. It’s about selling a narrative.
Pan Masala sells pleasure. Betting apps sell hope. Coaching centres sell success. All three sell dreams — and they all come at a cost.

text:
Final Thought
If you’re uncomfortable reading this — good. Because maybe, just maybe, that discomfort is where real questions begin.

title: Before We Blame the Next Generation, Let’s Look in the Mirror
text:
There’s a recurring narrative I keep noticing—especially from us, the so-called “Golden Generation,” the 80s-90s kids.
We proudly talk about how we had the best childhood, the best movies and music, the most unforgettable school and college days, and even a better environment. We say the newer generations—Millennials, Gen Z, and even younger—have only technology.
And then we go further: “They lack discipline.” “They don’t have manners, morals, or ethics.” “They have no respect for work, seniors, or even themselves.”
I’ll admit—I used to nod in agreement.
But then I paused. Who exactly are these Millennials and Gen Z? They are our younger siblings, our nieces and nephews, our own children, our students, our juniors at work.
And that raised a harder question: If something’s missing in them, who failed them? Isn’t it us?
I once read: “A child’s mind is like a blank canvas. What colour it takes depends on those who paint on it.”
So I ask: What colours did we paint?
Did we model integrity, or did we glorify success at any cost? Did we teach values, or just push for results? Did we justify bribery, shortcuts, and silencing others for personal gain—so long as it looked like success?
In our rush to give them a “better” life, maybe we led them through doors we never should have opened. And perhaps worse—we simply weren’t around. Ironically, those who were supposed to guide them—parents, teachers, elders—were often the ones least involved in meaningful, value-based interactions, by choice or by design.
And now, when they look for guidance, they turn to celebrities, influencers, and content creators—because those are the ones engaging with them more than we ever did.
So before we keep tagging this generation as “lost, entitled or misguided” let’s pause and ask:

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
text:
Whenever we hear the term mangrove restoration, the first image that usually comes to mind is quite simple: people standing on a mudflat, planting mangrove seedlings.
It is a positive image. It shows participation, effort and, more importantly, intent. But the more I work with coastal landscapes, the more I feel that this image represents only one part of restoration. In many cases, planting is probably not where the real work begins.
The real work begins much earlier, with trying to understand the landscape.

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: Why should a mangrove survive here?
text:
Why should a mangrove survive here?
This is probably one of the first questions we should ask before deciding where to plant. A mudflat may look uniform when we stand on it. From a distance, it may simply appear as one continuous open surface. But environmentally, it may not be uniform at all.
A slight difference in elevation, the way tidal water enters and leaves, how long water remains in an area, whether the sediment is stable or loose, salinity conditions, exposure, drainage and existing vegetation can all change within relatively short distances. To us, it may be the same mudflat. To a mangrove seedling, it may be a completely different environment.
That is where the distinction between planting mangroves and restoring mangroves becomes important.
Planting asks: Where can we put the seedlings?
Restoration asks: Why should they survive there, and what needs to be functioning in that landscape for them to survive naturally?

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: Sometimes the problem may not be the absence of trees
text:
Sometimes the problem may not be the absence of trees
We often see a bare coastal area and immediately think that vegetation needs to be introduced. But an open intertidal area is not necessarily an empty or degraded landscape.
Mudflats, tidal creeks, shallow water areas, saltmarshes and mangrove patches can all be parts of the same coastal system. Trying to convert every available open space into a plantation can therefore become problematic. Some areas may genuinely require intervention. Some may recover naturally if the environmental conditions are protected. Some may require restoration of water connectivity or other site conditions before planting is even considered. And some areas may simply need to be left alone.
I think this is one of the more important shifts required in restoration thinking. The question should not always be “Where can we plant?” Sometimes the better question is “What is this landscape trying to do naturally?”

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: GIS and remote sensing can tell us much more than where to plant
text:
GIS and remote sensing can tell us much more than where to plant
When GIS or remote sensing is mentioned in restoration projects, it is often associated with producing maps: suitable area, unsuitable area, plantation zone, priority zone.
Those outputs are useful, but I think their real value lies deeper. They help us understand how the landscape has behaved, not just how it looks at one point in time.
Satellite images allow us to look back and examine how the shoreline has changed, where vegetation persisted or disappeared, where channels shifted, where sediment accumulated, and whether an area that appears stable today has actually changed repeatedly over the years. Terrain data can help us understand elevation differences that may not be obvious in the field, while field observations tell us where our interpretation from satellite data was correct and where it was not.
Soil and sediment observations add another layer. Hydrology adds another. Local knowledge adds yet another. Individually, none of these tells the full story. Together, they begin to describe how the landscape actually functions.
For me, this is where geospatial analysis becomes particularly useful, not because it can always give us a final answer, but because it can help us ask better questions.

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: A map should also show us what we do not know
text:
A map should also show us what we do not know
This is something I have started appreciating more through project work. There is always a temptation to make a final map look definitive.
Green means suitable. Red means unsuitable. Yellow means moderate.
Simple, clean and easy to communicate.
But natural systems are rarely that clean. There are places where the available information is not enough, locations where field conditions do not match what we initially interpreted, and areas where seasonal behaviour may completely change how we understand the site.
Sometimes the correct conclusion may simply be: we need more information before intervening.
That uncertainty should not be treated as a weakness. In many cases, recognising uncertainty is probably more responsible than forcing an answer from incomplete data. A useful restoration map should therefore not only tell us where intervention appears possible. It should also tell us where verification is needed, where uncertainty is high, and where intervention may carry unnecessary risk.

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: And then there are the people who live with the landscape
text:
And then there are the people who live with the landscape
Technical assessments can become very data-heavy very quickly: satellite imagery, elevation models, hydrology, sediment, salinity, vegetation indices, field measurements. All of these matter.
But coastal landscapes are not just physical systems. They are also lived landscapes.
People fish there, travel through them, collect resources and observe seasonal changes. They notice when a tidal creek becomes shallower, when sediment begins accumulating in a particular area, when vegetation disappears, or when an earlier plantation survives in one location but fails completely in another.
That knowledge may never appear clearly in a satellite image.
This does not mean local observations should replace scientific assessment, nor should scientific assessment dismiss local observations. The more useful approach is probably to allow both to inform each other. Local observations can tell us where to look more carefully, geospatial data can place those observations in a wider spatial or temporal context, and field verification can test whether our interpretation actually holds.

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: Restoration, then, becomes a process rather than an event
text:
Restoration, then, becomes a process rather than an event
Instead of thinking:
Plant → Protect
I increasingly see restoration as something closer to:
Observe → Understand → Decide → Intervene → Monitor → Learn
That final part, learn, matters because our original assumptions may turn out to be wrong. A site that looked suitable may perform poorly. A place we expected to struggle may recover naturally. A planted patch may survive, but natural regeneration around it may remain absent. A hydrological intervention may alter the landscape differently from what was anticipated.
Monitoring should not simply confirm whether a project succeeded. It should also tell us whether our understanding of the landscape was correct. And if it was not, then the restoration strategy should be allowed to change.

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
section: Planting numbers are easy. Restoration success is harder.
text:
Planting numbers are easy. Restoration success is harder.
Numbers communicate well. Ten thousand seedlings planted. Fifty hectares covered. One lakh propagules distributed. They sound substantial, and they are easy to report.
But they do not necessarily tell us whether an ecosystem is recovering.
A smaller intervention carried out in an environmentally appropriate location may sometimes achieve much more than a larger plantation implemented without understanding site conditions. So perhaps the more meaningful questions are whether the plants are surviving and growing, whether natural recruitment is beginning, whether tidal processes are functioning properly, whether the substrate remains stable, whether the area is becoming ecologically self-sustaining, and whether the local community remains connected to the restoration process.
Those questions take longer to answer, but they probably tell us much more.

title: Why understanding the landscape matters in mangrove restoration
text:
Before we plant
I am not arguing against mangrove plantation. Planting can be an important restoration intervention.
But it should come after understanding the landscape, not before it.
The objective should not be to make every exposed coastal surface green. It should be to understand what that landscape can support, what it should retain, what has been disturbed, and where intervention is actually required.
Sometimes restoration may mean planting. Sometimes it may mean protecting natural regeneration. Sometimes it may mean correcting an environmental constraint. And sometimes it may mean leaving an area undisturbed.
Perhaps, then, the success of mangrove restoration should not ultimately be measured only by how many propagules we put into the ground. It should also be measured by how well we understood the landscape before we put them there, and how carefully we continued listening to it afterwards.
If you are involved in mangrove plantation or restoration work, I would be interested to know how you approach this.
What do you think of looking at restoration this way, with site understanding coming before intervention?
And beyond the aspects I have mentioned here, what else do you think should be considered before deciding whether to plant, restore hydrology, support natural regeneration, or simply leave an area undisturbed?
I would be especially interested in perspectives from people working directly in the field, because these decisions often become much more complicated once we move from maps and plans to the actual landscape.

Originally published on LinkedIn, 1 October 2026.

title: What does a satellite measure when we map NO₂?
text:
Reading this carefully

Shows

Tropospheric NO₂ vertical column density: the total amount in a column from the surface to the tropopause.

Doesn’t show

How that NO₂ is distributed vertically, or what people breathe at street level.

Connected to

Emission sources (traffic, industry, power generation), wind and vertical mixing, photochemistry, and meteorology. Together they set how a column amount relates to air at street level.
Satellite observations are widely used to study atmospheric pollutants over large areas. One of them is nitrogen dioxide, commonly associated with traffic, industry and power generation. With TROPOMI on Sentinel-5P we can map NO₂ over cities, industrial regions and whole countries.
But what exactly are we measuring?
Looking at a satellite NO₂ map, it is easy to assume the values are concentrations near the ground, like those from an air quality monitor. They are not. TROPOMI observes sunlight that has interacted with the atmosphere and surface. Retrieval algorithms use that spectral information to estimate the NO₂ in the atmospheric column. For tropospheric products, the result is a vertical column density, usually in molecules/cm² or mol/m², not a concentration at a given height.

title: What does a satellite measure when we map NO₂?
text:
Why the distinction matters
NO₂ depends on emissions, but also on wind, mixing, chemistry and weather. Two places can have similar column amounts but different near-surface concentrations, depending on how the gas is distributed vertically. A higher column does not automatically mean proportionally worse air at breathing height.
Satellite data is still extremely valuable for regional patterns, changes over time and likely emission hotspots, especially where ground monitors are sparse. Understanding near-surface air quality needs more: ground observations, meteorology and, depending on the question, atmospheric models.
Before interpreting a satellite map, know what the values represent.

title: Low-chlorophyll waters are spreading in the tropical Indian Ocean
text:
Reading this carefully

Shows

Changes in the spatial extent of low-chlorophyll waters during 2015–2024, with physical and biogeochemical changes occurring alongside.

Doesn’t show

Established causal pathways. Associations are not mechanisms, and interannual climate modes overlap the study period.

Connected to

Surface warming and stratification, nutrient supply to the surface, monsoon circulation and freshwater input, and interannual modes such as El Niño and the Indian Ocean Dipole.



Low-chlorophyll regions are a natural feature of the open ocean. These oligotrophic waters have relatively low phytoplankton biomass and cover large parts of the tropical oceans. But do their boundaries stay put, or are they changing?
That was one of the questions in our recently published study on the tropical Indian Ocean, 2015–2024. Instead of asking only whether chlorophyll-a increased or decreased at particular locations, we looked at how the extent of low-chlorophyll water changed over the decade.
The tropical Indian Ocean is interesting here because its regions behave so differently. The Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and southern Indian Ocean respond differently to monsoons, circulation and freshwater input, so chlorophyll varies considerably by region and season.
We used satellite chlorophyll-a with sea-surface temperature and salinity, and examined ocean reanalysis data on nutrients, dissolved oxygen, pCO₂ and pH.
The result was not simply chlorophyll declining everywhere. Expansion differed by region and season. At the same time the ocean environment was changing: widespread surface warming, a noticeable oxygen decline in the Bay of Bengal, rising pCO₂ and falling pH in the datasets analysed. The period also included major El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole events, so interpreting decadal patterns meant accounting for that interannual variability.



Conceptual graphic of the study context. Not satellite data, measured boundaries or quantitative results.


Paper: Expansion of low-chlorophyll regions in the tropical Indian Ocean: spatial patterns and physical–biogeochemical associations. Marine and Freshwater Research 77(15), MF26083 (2026). doi:10.1071/MF26083

title: Southeast Asia’s haze: fires and forecasts together
text:
Reading this carefully

Shows

How CAMS forecasts expected aerosol conditions to evolve over 14–19 October 2026, set against fires observed the week before.

Doesn’t show

Smoke-plume trajectories. Fire locations and high aerosol together do not establish a transport pathway, and the arrows are modelled 10 m winds.

Connected to

Fire activity and emission strength, winds at several atmospheric levels, vertical mixing, and removal by rainfall. The forecast model represents these; this visualisation does not separate them.
Forest and vegetation fires are important contributors to atmospheric aerosol loading, particularly where seasonal biomass burning affects air quality across national boundaries. Southeast Asia is one such region, and understanding where aerosols are and how they may move requires more than finding the fires.
I put together a small visualisation integrating satellite-derived active-fire detections with atmospheric composition forecasts, to look at how aerosol conditions might evolve across the region.

title: Southeast Asia’s haze: fires and forecasts together
text:
Data


Fires

NASA FIRMS (VIIRS) active-fire detections, 7–14 October 2026

Forecasts

Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service: five-day forecasts of total AOD, organic matter AOD, surface PM₂.₅ and near-surface winds, initialised 14 October 2026

Terrain

GEBCO 2026

Processing

Python and GIS libraries, animated at six-hour intervals

title: Southeast Asia’s haze: fires and forecasts together
text:
What the forecasts indicated
Across the study region, modelled mean total AOD decreases by about 43.5% over the five days, and organic matter AOD by about 49%. The reduction is not uniform: areas of elevated aerosol remain in parts of equatorial Southeast Asia even as the regional mean falls. The fire detections give useful geographical context for where organic aerosol loading is enhanced.

title: Southeast Asia’s haze: fires and forecasts together
text:
What it doesn’t establish
Identifying active fires and observing elevated aerosol does not by itself establish a transport pathway between them. The wind vectors are modelled 10 m winds, while aerosol transport happens across several atmospheric levels. This is an illustration of forecast evolution in relation to observed fires, not a reconstruction of smoke plumes.
The broader aim was to see how several Earth observation and modelling datasets can be combined to communicate a regional process, while staying clear about what each dataset represents.
The animation shows model forecasts, not observed future air quality. Fire detections are historical observations. Data: CAMS/ECMWF, NASA FIRMS, GEBCO Compilation Group (2026).

title: About
text:
I believe all research, whatever its scale, should be transparent about its method and honest about its results, positive or negative. Every contribution becomes reference material for someone else at some point. If the foundation is fragile, whatever is built on it will fail sooner or later, however carefully it is built.
So in everything I do, I try to show the whole picture. Work like this is not always publishable, but it can still be shared. This site is partly a record of those efforts, kept for whoever builds on them next, including me.
I also want to bring context back into environmental work. Many polished maps, posts and project reports show an outcome without the system around it. No environmental change happens in isolation. I don’t try to trace every connection, but I name the dominant ones, so readers know what else might be shaping a result.

Your data

title: Two NDVI maps are not the whole story
text:
Reading this carefully

Shows

Post-monsoon NDVI across Ahmedabad was higher in 2025 than in 2017, and dry-season NDVI stayed fairly stable.

Doesn’t show

A steady trend, or what caused the change. This is a methods illustration, not a trend test or attribution study.

Connected to

Rainfall and monsoon timing, crop and vegetation phenology, irrigation and soil moisture, and land-cover change from urban expansion. None were tested here; each could explain part of the signal.
Recently I’ve been seeing quite a few posts where NDVI maps from two different years are placed side by side, and the difference is immediately read as improving or declining vegetation. Sometimes that change is then linked to plantation, restoration, development or degradation.
There is nothing wrong with comparing NDVI between two periods. The problem begins when the comparison itself becomes the conclusion. A higher NDVI in the second image does not automatically mean permanent vegetation gain, and a lower one does not necessarily mean loss.

title: Two NDVI maps are not the whole story
section: Questions to ask before reading two maps
text:
Questions to ask before reading two maps

Were both images acquired in the same season?
Are they single-date scenes, monthly, seasonal or annual composites?
Were the sensor, masking, resolution and colour scale the same?
Were rainfall and moisture conditions comparable?
And the one that is easiest to miss: what happened in the years between them?




The two endpoint maps and the annual pathway between them. Same October–November window and NDVI display scale throughout.


If I compare only post-monsoon NDVI from 2017 and 2025, 2025 clearly looks greener. If those were the only two images shown, it would be easy to call this an increase in vegetation over time.
Once the intervening years are added, the picture changes. Post-monsoon NDVI rose sharply in 2019, dropped in 2020, rose again in 2021, eased over the following years and rose again by 2025. The endpoint difference is real, but the pathway was not a smooth increase.

title: Two NDVI maps are not the whole story
text:
Seasonality complicates it further
In the same series, pre-monsoon NDVI stayed comparatively stable while post-monsoon NDVI varied much more from year to year. Compare unmatched seasonal windows, or choose dates without thinking about rainfall and phenology, and the apparent change can look very different from the longer pattern.



Post-monsoon NDVI, 2017–2025, with 2026 shown as early post-monsoon (1 September to 4 October), so not directly equivalent.





Pre-monsoon NDVI (April–May), 2017–2026. The dry-season series stays comparatively constrained.





Seasonal greening amplitude varies from year to year, another reason not to mix unmatched windows.



Two NDVI maps can both be correct while the story built from them is incomplete.

For researchers and students the practical lesson is simple: compare like with like, keep the processing consistent, and if the argument is about change over time, look at the years in between.
For planners and decision-makers shown before-and-after NDVI maps, two questions go a long way. Were these images actually comparable? And what happened in between?
One of the great strengths of remote sensing is repeated observation of the same landscape over time. It seems wasteful to have that time series and then reduce the interpretation to two convenient snapshots.

title: From Trichodesmium in the water to signals from space
text:
Reading this carefully

Shows

Which absorption-guided spectral relationships survive from hyperspectral to multispectral resolution, and how a Trichodesmium Spectral Index (TSI) behaves spatially.

Doesn’t show

Bloom detection from a single absorption feature. Mixed communities, varying biomass and coastal optics all complicate the signal.

Connected to

Mixed phytoplankton communities, wide variation in biomass, and the optical complexity of coastal waters. Each can blur or mimic the bloom signal.



Our earlier work on phytoplankton typing off Kochi started with a simple question: can pigment-related features in absorption spectra still carry useful information when we move to satellite observations? That work combined microscopy, HPLC pigments, phytoplankton absorption and satellite reflectance. Fourth-derivative absorption analysis identified spectral features linked to changes in community composition, which we then explored at multispectral satellite resolution.
In our more recent work we applied that absorption-guided approach to Trichodesmium blooms in the Arabian Sea.
Here the problem was more specific. Trichodesmium has characteristic phycobiliprotein absorption, but detecting a bloom from space is not just a matter of finding one feature. Natural waters hold mixed communities, biomass varies widely, and coastal waters add optical complexity.
So we followed the signal through several stages: field-observed blooms, pigment composition, phytoplankton absorption, hyperspectral reflectance, MODIS-Aqua bands, and finally satellite-scale spatial patterns. Hyperspectral observations were convolved with MODIS-Aqua spectral response functions, and the relationships still detectable at multispectral resolution were used to build the TSI. We then compared its spatial behaviour with chlorophyll-a and used spatial analysis to distinguish cyanobacterial hotspots from other high-biomass waters.



Conceptual figure of the workflow, from the earlier coastal work to the Trichodesmium application. Spectra, pigments and imagery are illustrative, not study data.


Paper: Optical variability of Trichodesmium erythraeum and T. thiebautii blooms in the Arabian Sea: from pigments to satellite signals. Remote Sensing Applications: Society and Environment 43, 102251 (2026). doi:10.1016/j.rsase.2026.102251

title: Bridging the Gap: Adapting to Students’ Perspectives in Teaching
text:
In a recent interview (in which I flunked ;) ), I faced a scenario that made me reflect on my teaching approach. I was asked to guide a child through a basic math operation: “Subtract 15 from 5.” The child’s response was 15 - 5 = 10, highlighting a fundamental misunderstanding.
My task was to explain that the operation should be 5 - 15, not the other way around. I attempted to use the example of toffees to illustrate the concept. Still, I became so focused on explaining positive and negative numbers that I lost sight of my primary goal. I’m grateful to the interviewer for pointing out this gap in my approach and providing valuable feedback on improving.
As both a student and a teacher, I’ve encountered numerous situations where communication breaks down due to differing perspectives. Teachers must adapt their explanations to align with the child’s understanding and help them navigate their learning challenges.

title: Conflicts - Not an Obstruction but a Learning Curve
text:
A classroom is a society itself, a microcosm where you have friendship, rivalry, misunderstandings, separations, reunions and conflicts. It’s a space to learn about the world and also about oneself. We have a curriculum for the world and beyond. But how do we help children learn about themselves and evolve? This is done by utilizing their day to day experiences and guiding them to find their own way through those experiences.
The same goes when there’s a conflict in that microcosmic society. When we contain a conflict and just brush it aside, we are limiting a rich learning opportunity for them. Here we can show them how to disagree without demeaning, how to express without hurting and what to do to earn back a broken trust.

title: Conflicts - Not an Obstruction but a Learning Curve
text:
When Conflict Becomes the Teacher
If someone asked me what’s the most important topic that is not a part of our curriculum - I’d say The Language of Emotions - a way to express oneself. Children should ideally learn it through experience. But in today’s world who has the time to reflect on experiences? Disagreements in classrooms often arise not from malice but from confusion, immaturity or unmet needs. A sarcastic remark is used to hide insecurity and a sudden push is used to express what words cannot.
Rather than viewing conflicts as a disruption or misbehaving, teachers can reframe them as emotional data. Try asking “What made you do that or behave that way?” instead of “Who started it?” The focus shifts from blame to understanding. It is not about taking sides but discovering the story behind an action or reaction.

title: Conflicts - Not an Obstruction but a Learning Curve
section: Teacher - Not a Judge but a Facilitator
text:
Teacher - Not a Judge but a Facilitator
The culmination of a classroom conflict is decided by the teacher’s response. In that moment, we as teachers should be clear about the fact that, we are not here to judge the children but to facilitate them, to guide them.
The process begins by pausing the escalation and acknowledging the emotions of the children. Guide them to describe the incident through “I” statements - “I felt hurt when he/she …”. These reflections help the children to identify the underlying emotions. What follows will not be a forced apology or reconciliation but a genuine effort in rebuilding relationships.
Repeated practice helps students internalize this approach as a model for conflict transformation. They learn that empathy, when applied to real tensions, is not weakness but wisdom.

title: Conflicts - Not an Obstruction but a Learning Curve
section: Conflict Literacy as a Life Skill
text:
Conflict Literacy as a Life Skill
If reading, writing and numerical skills are fundamental in learning then managing disagreement with respect is an essential life skill. When open dialogues and emotional reflections are normalized, students stop fearing mistakes in relationships. Boundaries in relationships will be viewed as a healthy expression of individuality. Respect evolves from silent compliance to active consideration.
Conflict literacy prepares students for the world beyond the classroom, where empathy, responsibility, negotiation and accountability become the foundations of collaboration. In such a society, discipline ceases to be a system of punishment and becomes a daily practice in humanity.

title: Conflicts - Not an Obstruction but a Learning Curve
text:
From Chaos to Curriculum
Classrooms are not just literacy centers but a space for developing personalities as well. Imagine a classroom where a conflict is treated as a lesson in empathy. A quarrel over sharing becomes a discussion about fairness. Teasing transforms into a reflection on dignity. A group argument becomes a practice in democratic listening.
If we can approach these moments with curiosity instead of control, children will learn that conflict is not an agent of division but a medium to reforge relationships. Empathy is rarely built in calm. It is tested, refined and strengthened through conflicts.
True emotional maturity lies in recognizing that conflicts are not interruptions to learning, they are lessons themselves. The goal for us should not be in creating a conflict-free classroom, but a resilient one where students are guided to learn from conflicts, to evolve through them and carry those lessons into the world beyond school. In doing so, they not only grow as individuals but also shape a more empathetic society.

title: Strategies to Address Miscommunication and Misunderstandings in Children

title: Physics, Philosophy and Eminem
text:
Physics has always been an enigma to me. The more I tried to understand it, the more strange and fascinating it seemed. In my younger days, I went with the flow, focusing on good grades rather than grasping the content. I thought that once I got through school, I’d never need physics again, so why bother? But later, as I was exposed to more ideas and perspectives, a wonderful world opened up for me. While I still struggle with complex theories and formulas, it’s the simplest topics that have always captivated me.
Throughout my academic and professional life as a researcher and teacher, I realized that physics has a deeply philosophical side if you look at it from a different perspective. Teaching topics like vibrations and resonance made me reflect on how they mirror life. All we need is one external trigger that matches our frequency to produce the maximum output. Isn’t that what we’re all searching for? To find that one thing in life that brings out our best effort, no matter the resistance.
This idea connects deeply with Eminem’s song “Beautiful” (yes, I’m a fan!). We often try to match ourselves with others, seeking acceptance and fleeting happiness, only to lose sight of who we really are. In trying so hard to fit in, we miss the chance to find our own path. Eminem captures this beautifully.
The song’s message is simple: the path you were given fits you, so walk it with pride and don’t let anyone convince you otherwise.
Like in physics, where resonance occurs when an external force matches an object’s natural frequency, life’s purpose is finding what resonates with us. It’s about being true to ourselves, finding that unique frequency, and letting it guide us to our full potential.

Originally published on LinkedIn, 2 September 2024.

title: The Power of Understanding: Lessons from Taare Zameen Par That Shaped My Perspective
text:
“Why can’t you just behave?” This was a thought I often had when encountering frustration, anger, or mischievousness in others. My default reaction was irritation, not empathy—until a particular scene from Taare Zameen Par (2007) profoundly changed my outlook.
The scene where the art teacher, Ram Shankar Nikumbh, visits Ishaan’s home to uncover why a talented child is withering away, struck me deeply. When Ram asks Ishaan’s father to read a Chinese label, the father’s realization that his son’s struggles with dyslexia are as challenging as reading an unfamiliar language is eye-opening. At that moment, I began to understand the importance of looking beyond behavior to the underlying struggles.
Watching this as a teenager, I was moved to tears. It made me reflect on how quick I had been to judge others without considering what they might be going through. This scene taught me to pause, reflect, and ask, “What if?” What if there’s a deeper reason behind someone’s frustration or behavior?
As a teacher, this approach became invaluable. Instead of reacting to a student’s outbursts or mischief with frustration, I learned to look for the sadness or confusion behind their actions. This shift allowed me to address their issues more effectively and to be more patient and understanding in my interactions.
Even now, outside the classroom, I strive to maintain this perspective. Taking a moment to understand the person next to me has improved my relationships and enriched my perception of the world.
I sincerely hope this reflection inspires others to have that moment of patience and empathy to see beyond the surface, and better understand the world around them.

text:
With VIKAS Centre for Development, 2025 to present
Two strands of work support a long-running, community-based mangrove restoration programme on the Gujarat coast: looking back at what two decades of planting achieved, and building the baseline for the next phase.


An independent GIS assessment of restoration carried out in four phases: 2002–2012, 2013–2016, 2017–2020 and 2021–2023. The planted area was mapped as 59 polygon units across 30 regions, so that each could be tracked over time.


Imagery

Landsat 7 for the pre-restoration baseline (2000); Sentinel-2 for 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024

Indices

NDVI, OSAVI and EVI for vegetation condition and density classes; NDSI for surface salinity trends

Analyses

Change detection, area by density class, carbon sequestration estimates, shoreline change and salinity transects



About 2,900 hectares were brought under plantation. By 2024, about 1,650 hectares, roughly 57%, showed mangrove cover detectable from space: 752 ha dense, 628 ha moderate and 271 ha sparse.
That 57% is easy to misread. It does not mean the other 43% died. Mangroves take years to grow large and dense enough to stand out from the surrounding mudflat in 10 m Sentinel-2 pixels, and much of the area was planted recently. Splitting the result by phase makes this visible: detected cover is about 77% of the planted area for 2002–2012, 59% for 2013–2016, 31% for 2017–2020, and 13% for 2021–2023.



Planted area and satellite-detected mangrove cover by planting phase, Bharuch coast, as of 2024. Area in hectares.


The steady decline with younger phases fits growth time rather than failure, although stress from salinity, stagnation or poor tidal access also plays a part at some sites. The two cannot be fully separated from space. Reporting planted area, detected cover and planting age together is the point: the first is effort, the second is what the satellite can confirm, and the third explains much of the gap.

Reading this carefully

Shows

Where planted areas have developed mangrove cover, at what density, and how cover, surface salinity and the shoreline changed between 2000 and 2024.

Doesn’t show

Mortality. Undetected area is not dead area: young plantations are often too small or sparse to resolve at 10 m. Field survival counts are needed for that. Carbon figures are model-based estimates, and NDSI tracks a surface spectral signal, not measured soil salinity.

Connected to

Planting age and growth rate, tidal access and drainage, salinity, salt pan expansion along the coast, and industrial land use nearby.






For the Khambhat Mangrove Restoration Project, before large-scale planting at three new sites on the Bharuch coast (Tadatalav, Bajipura and Ralej), the question was where saplings could survive and where field teams could work safely. Public elevation data cannot resolve the few centimetres that decide whether water drains or stagnates on these mudflats, so the baseline tracked water behaviour directly.



Conceptual intertidal cross-section: how inundation frequency, the dominant environment and restoration potential change from land to channel, and how satellite, field and soil data are combined for planning. A conceptual illustration, not site data.


Approach. A two-year Sentinel-1 radar time series was used to map how often each part of the mudflats holds water, separating active tidal channels, stable corridors and stagnant depressions. Field verification checked those patterns on the ground, along with mud stability and safe access, and drew on local knowledge of seasonal access and channel changes; coastal residents provided tractors to cross unstable mud. Soil cores were analysed in a laboratory.
A negative result that changed the plan. Portable field probes suggested moderate salinity and patches of acidic soil. Laboratory analysis corrected both: the soils were alkaline throughout, and salinity in stagnant basins and on higher ground was far higher than the probes indicated, at levels that stress young mangroves severely. Field readings had been distorted by waterlogged, mineral-rich mud. Planting decisions based on the probes alone would have put saplings into soil likely to kill them.
The three sites turned out to be three different systems a few kilometres apart: Tadatalav, a well-flushed mudflat with lower salinity but deep, fluid mud; Bajipura, a trapped basin with firm but highly saline ground; and Ralej, a raised platform where conditions change sharply with elevation.
The recommendations moved away from uniform planting: restore drainage before planting in stagnant areas, cluster work in verified stable corridors, shift towards mixed species, and set worker-safety protocols for unstable mud. A post-monsoon reassessment is built into the plan.
The detailed methods and results may be published, so this summary leaves out specific thresholds and values.

Reading this carefully

Shows

How often each part of the sites is wet, where conditions are stable enough to plant and walk, and laboratory-verified soil conditions at sampled points.

Doesn’t show

Elevation itself, conditions during the monsoon, or sapling survival. The radar record covers two years, and soil chemistry is known only where cores were taken.

Connected to

Tidal flushing and channel siltation, evaporation, livestock grazing, and community use of the mudflats.









Recording observations at a tidal channel edge.







Taking a soil core on soft, waterlogged mud.









Labelling and logging samples with the field team.







Field kit testing on cracked, salt-crusted ground. Laboratory analysis later corrected readings like these.





Field verification, February–March 2026.

section: Brine outfall siting on an arid coastal mudflat
text:
Brine outfall siting on an arid coastal mudflat
Hydrodynamic assessment for an industrial client, western India, 2026
A proposed treatment plant needed a location to discharge brine onto a hyper-arid coastal mudflat without the effluent reaching a nearby embankment or salt-working areas, now or across the seasons. The task was to find where the water would go, and whether it would stay there.


Field survey

DGPS micro-elevation transects, soil cores and in-situ conductivity. The site is clay-rich, hypersaline, salt-crusted and almost impermeable, with less than half a metre of relief across the area.

Terrain

ALOS AW3D30 surface model, cleaned and conditioned in Google Earth Engine

Model

HEC-RAS 2D on a 30 m mesh. The diffusion-wave solver was chosen after a control run showed results matching the full shallow-water equations in this friction-dominated, slow-flow setting. A 10 m mesh captured finer channels but became numerically unstable over a full year.

Forcing

13 months of daily CHIRPS rainfall and ERA5-Land evapotranspiration (February 2025 to February 2026)

Design load

Discharge set 50% above the maximum design capacity, pulsed to mimic operating and maintenance cycles



Siting. A worst-case run with no rainfall and no evaporation showed the effluent stays confined to natural micro-channels, so subtle topography controls where it goes. Five candidate outfall points were then tested. Four routed effluent towards the embankment. One, about 600 m from the original proposal, sits behind a micro-divide only tens of centimetres high that stops westward flow and sends the discharge down an eastward gradient, away from both sensitive areas.
Seasonal behaviour at the chosen point. In the dry season, evaporation balances the discharge and the wetted area stays within local channels. During the monsoon, regional flooding submerges the outfall entirely; water levels rise under constant inflow, which shows the regional flood, not the discharge, controls levels then. After the monsoon, evaporation removes the standing water, and by late winter the footprint returns to its dry-season extent with no carry-over to the next year.
Recommendations included passive relief drains for extreme monsoon ponding, contingency relief wells, and a monitoring plan (drone surveys, salinity measurements and post-monsoon inundation mapping) so field behaviour can be checked against the model.

Reading this carefully

Shows

Where discharged water flows and pools across a full seasonal cycle, under conservative loading, and which outfall location keeps it away from sensitive areas.

Doesn’t show

Salinity transport, density-driven mixing between brine and floodwater, or wind-driven spreading. Terrain is held static, so post-monsoon reshaping and features smaller than 30 m are not captured.

Connected to

Monsoon rainfall and regional flooding, evaporation, micro-topography, and future changes to the surrounding land use.

M.Phil. dissertation, 2013. For my M.Phil. in Ecological Informatics at IIITM-K, Thiruvananthapuram, I carried out the dissertation at ATREE, Bangalore. It assessed the impact of urbanisation on wetlands in Kochi Corporation and surrounding panchayats between 1990 and 2010, using Landsat TM and IRS LISS-III imagery, normalised difference indices and a test index developed to separate built-up from barren land.
